items.title: Albert Burbank Interview, 1959-03-18
items.q: So I tried to get Lorenzo Teo to teach me. I went to Lorenzo's house. And he agreed to teach me.

ctx.x: Did anybody have a banging system at all in those days that you knew?

Not that I know of, you know. Mm-hmm. And, um, well I took it and tried to practice on it. I didn't know what I was doing. So I tried to get Lorenzo Teo to teach me. I went to Lorenzo's house. He was staying on Seminar Street. I went to Lorenzo's house. And he agreed to teach me. He told me, he said, he told me to go buy a book. I told Angie and come to his house the following Wednesday.
Is that the young Lorenzo Teo? Yes.

items.title: Albert Burbank Interview, 1959-03-18
items.q: INTERVIEWER: 'Lorenzo Junior, I guess. He was my favorite.' / INTERVIEWEE: 'He was your favorite.'

ctx.x: Mostly, yeah. They, they, they, they'd get to, they'd get the music of a number and run over until they get it in the head and then put it aside.

Can you tell us some more about the very earliest musicians, especially the clarinet players that you heard, just what style they played, that is, if there was any difference in the style of Big Eye and say Piku or, of course I've heard both of them too, or the Teos. I never did get to hear any of the Teos. He was great. Lorenzo Junior, I guess. He was my favorite.
